prompt: Where did the cluster keep the list of pods behind the Service `shop`?
hint: A separate object, kept by a controller.

choices.text: In the Service's own `spec`
choices.why: The Service holds a selector; the list of addresses is another object.

choices.text: In an EndpointSlice
choices.why: Right: three addresses on port 8080, matching the three pods.

choices.text: In CoreDNS, as one record per pod
choices.why: The Service's name resolves to its one ClusterIP, not to the pods.

choices.text: In the kube-proxy pod on the control plane
choices.why: kube-proxy reads the list on every node; it does not keep it.

prompt: Inside a pod in the `default` namespace, why does the bare name `shop` reach the Service?

choices.text: Every Service is published under its bare name on the internet
choices.why: Cluster names never leave the cluster; the lab's DNS answers nothing outside `cluster.local`.

choices.text: kube-proxy rewrites the name into an address
choices.why: kube-proxy works on addresses, never on names.

choices.text: The resolver's search list adds `default.svc.cluster.local`
choices.why: Right: `shop` becomes `shop.default.svc.cluster.local`, which CoreDNS knows.

choices.text: The pod's `/etc/hosts` lists every Service
choices.why: Services are resolved by CoreDNS at `10.96.0.10`, not by a file.

prompt: A Service's name resolves, but every call to it is refused at once. `kubectl get endpointslices` shows `<unset>`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: An empty list behind a working address.

choices.text: CoreDNS is down
choices.why: The name resolved, so CoreDNS answered.

choices.text: kube-proxy is not running on that node
choices.why: The slice is empty before kube-proxy even reads it.

choices.text: Its selector matches no ready pod
choices.why: Right: no pods, or a label typo, leaves the slice empty and the address refusing.

choices.text: The Service's ClusterIP changed after it was created
choices.why: A Service's address never changes while it exists.

prompt: The full name of the Service `shop` in the namespace `default` is `shop.default.___.cluster.local`.
A NodePort Service has `nodePort: 30080`. Which nodes answer on port 30080?
hint: The first curl asked a worker by its address.

choices.text: Only the nodes running a pod of it
choices.why: Every node answers by default; lesson 17 shows the setting that narrows it.

choices.text: Every node
choices.why: Right, whether a pod runs there or not.

choices.text: Only the control-plane node
choices.why: `shop-worker` answered directly.

choices.text: Whichever node the scheduler picks for the Service
choices.why: A Service is never scheduled; it is not a pod.

prompt: The LoadBalancer Service `shop-lb` showed `80:31269/TCP` besides its external address. What is `31269`?
hint: A LoadBalancer is built on another type.

choices.text: The port the shop listens on inside the pod
choices.why: The shop listens on 8080.

choices.text: A port on the laptop
choices.why: It is a port on every node of the cluster.

choices.text: The NodePort that the balancer sends its traffic to
choices.why: Right. A LoadBalancer is a NodePort with a balancer in front.

choices.text: The balancer's administration port
choices.why: That is internal to the balancer and not in the Service.

prompt: A team on a cloud has forty web applications and wants each reachable from the internet. Why do most clusters use one LoadBalancer Service and an ingress controller instead of forty LoadBalancer Services?
hint: What does each LoadBalancer Service ask the cloud for?

choices.text: Kubernetes allows only one LoadBalancer per cluster
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: Each one is a balancer billed by the hour
choices.why: Right: one balancer in front of one controller routes all forty by host and path.

choices.text: LoadBalancer Services cannot use port 80
choices.why: `shop-lb` answered on port 80.

choices.text: Ingress is faster than a LoadBalancer
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the Ingress controller sits behind a LoadBalancer anyway.

prompt: Order the Service types from the one with the fewest ways in to the one with the most.
hint: Each is built on the one before.
trap: A NodePort includes a ClusterIP, and a LoadBalancer includes a NodePort.
